newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia sees aviation pact with U.S. by April.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sees aviation pact with U.S. by April.

text.p: Malaysia and the United States are expected to conclude an aviation pact allowing unrestricted access by airlines of the two countries before April, Malaysian Transport Minister Ling Liong Sik said.
Ling told reporters in the west coast city of Malacca that negotiations with Washington are going well and should be concluded within two months, the New Straits Times reported on Sunday.
The United States concluded a similar pact with Singapore earlier this week in Washington.

U.S. officials had said they hoped the deal with Singapore would be the first of a series of open skies agreements aimed at easing restrictions between the United States and Asia, the world's fastest growing market.
Ling said the discussions with the United States began during a visit by U.S. Transportation Secretary Frederico Pena to Malaysia late last year and had proceeded very well.
"The ministry does not foresee any hitches in the agreement as most of the problems between both sides have been ironed out," the New Straits Times quoted him as saying.
At present, national carrier Malaysian Airline System Bhd flies only to Los Angeles six times a week.
The pact would allow Malaysia to fly anywhere in the United States with no restrictions on flight frequencies, destinations and the size of aircraft, Ling said.
U.S. carriers would have the same rights in Malaysia.

In principle, open skies agreements also call for unlimited "beyond rights" which would allow U.S. airlines to pick up passengers or cargo in the country with which it had such an agreement and fly to any other country.
It was not clear from Ling's comments if such rights would be included in the agreement with Malaysia.

The United States also held open skies talks with Japan on January 10 and 11. Japanese officials have argued that an existing U.S.-Japanese airline accord was weighted in favour of the United States and an open skies accord would only increase the dominance of U.S. carriers.
The United States last year struck a series of open skies deals with Canada, Germany and other European countries. Talks are also being held with Britain, but so far with little progress.
